title: Kiko Walks His Own Way
summary: Kiko, a little crab, wants to walk straight like everyone else on the beach. Until a seagull shows him, from up in the sky, what his footsteps leave behind.

scenes.text:
On a golden beach lived a small red crab called Kiko.

Kiko had two claws that he waved all the time, as if he were saying hello, and eight legs that always went the same way.

Sideways.

Because that's how crabs walk. But Kiko didn't know that, because there was no other crab on that beach but him.

The snail went straight ahead. The fish swam straight ahead. Estela the starfish moved so little that she didn't count, but if she had moved, she would surely have gone straight.

"I'm the only one who walks crooked," sighed Kiko.

The next day, Kiko decided to learn to walk straight.

He pointed his claws forward. He stared at the rock in front of him. He pushed with all his legs and…

Off he went, sideways.

He tried again, harder. His legs got all tangled up, and Kiko landed on his tummy in the sand. Flump!

He tried all morning. Towards the rock, towards the water, towards the dune. And always, always, he ended up going sideways, or on his tummy, or spinning round like a top.

In the end he sat down, covered in sand right up to his eyes.

"I'm no good at walking," he said.

Just then, down onto the rock to rest came a seagull.

"Hey, crab," she said. "Do you know who made that drawing?"

"What drawing?"

"That one, in the sand. From up there you can see the whole thing. It's the prettiest thing I've ever seen on this beach."

Kiko looked around. From down here, all he could see were little heaps of sand and squiggles.

"Climb on," she said.

Kiko held on to her feathers with his claws, without squeezing, and up she flew.

Up and up they went, until the beach was tiny.

And then Kiko saw it.

On the golden sand there was an enormous drawing. There were zigzag paths, and curves, and curls, and little flowers where he had landed on his tummy. It ran from the water to the dune, like a colourful ribbon.

They were his tracks.

All the crooked steps of the whole morning.

"Did I… did I make that?" asked Kiko.

"Who else?" said the white bird. "Nobody else on this beach walks like that."

From that day on, Kiko draws.

Every morning he goes down to the shore, looks at the smooth sand and thinks about what he's going to make. A fish. A snail. A sun with a smiley face. A star for Estela, who doesn't move but sees everything.

He walks sideways, this way and that, and the sand fills up with drawings.

The snail comes to look. The fish peek out of the water. And his feathered friend flies over to see them from above, which is the best way.

In the afternoon, the sea creeps up and rubs them out with a wave.

But Kiko doesn't mind. Tomorrow the beach will be blank again, waiting for his footsteps.
